planting.note: Pot divisions in a shallow container of fast-draining succulent mix, since the slender cylindrical leaves rise from a compact clustering base rather than a wide-spreading rhizome.

directions: This African species produces slender, nearly cylindrical leaves marked by shallow longitudinal grooves that create soft rounded ridges rather than the smooth round canes of true cylindrica types. It tolerates deep interior shade and sporadic watering about as well as any snake plant, making it a forgiving choice for low-light corners, though a few hours of bright indirect light each day keeps the fan more upright and compact. Let the gritty succulent mix dry out completely between waterings, since the thick leaves hold enough moisture to shrug off weeks of neglect but rot quickly if kept damp. In late winter or early spring, established clumps can send up a spike of small white, sweetly fragrant flowers.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set divisions in a wide, heavy pot with gritty succulent mix for stability, since each growth point produces a few very large leaves rather than many small fans.

directions: Native to West Africa and the Central African Republic, this species grows as a single upright shoot of a few massive, leathery leaves rather than the clustering rosettes typical of trifasciata, so each plant reads more like a single bold sculptural blade. Mature leaves are marked with light green transverse striping on a darker green background, and the margins develop a distinctive reddish-brown edge as the leaf ages. Because individual leaves can reach several feet in length even in a container, give it a wide, heavy pot for stability and expect slow but steady growth in deep shade or bright indirect light alike. Water only once the fast-draining mix has dried fully, as with other Sansevieria the leathery leaves store ample moisture and are far more vulnerable to rot from overwatering than to drought.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow in a small, shallow pot of gritty succulent mix in filtered light, dividing offsets only once they have formed their own roots.

directions: This East African and Madagascan species forms a loose cluster of short, thick, nearly cylindrical leaves that curve and twist in an irregular, almost haphazard pattern, with grey-green coloring overlaid by pale mottled flecking. It grows slowly and stays compact, which suits small pots and tabletop displays better than the taller strap-leaved Sansevieria types. Give it mostly shade to filtered light and keep it above 50 degrees Fahrenheit, since it is noticeably more cold-sensitive than hardier trifasciata forms. Water sparingly, letting the gritty mix dry out completely between waterings, and expect showy white flower spikes on well-established plants.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide at the rhizome in spring and pot singly or in small groups in fast-draining succulent mix, since each growth point carries only one or two broad leaves.

directions: This species typically produces just one or two erect to slightly recurved, strap-shaped leaves per growth point, each far broader and more leathery than a single trifasciata fan division, giving mature specimens a bold, minimal silhouette. Juvenile leaves carry striking irregular pale yellow-green transverse bands or elongated blotches across a darker green surface, a pattern that fades with age but remains attractive for years. Native to a wide swath of East Africa from Sudan to Zambia, it shares the genus's tolerance for deep shade and infrequent watering, and thrives in the same bright-to-shady windowsill conditions suited to common snake plants. Allow the fast-draining succulent mix to dry out completely between waterings, since root and rhizome rot from overwatering remain the primary risks to an otherwise trouble-free houseplant.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
